source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task
finding: Founding 2-4-6 rule discovery task. People got 2,4,6, proposed their own triples, and were told yes or no. The true rule was any three numbers in increasing order. Most tested only triples that fit their own narrower guess, so they kept getting yes and announced wrong rules.
numbers: N=29 psychology undergraduates (17 men, 12 women), tested alone, 45-minute cap. 6 reached the correct rule with no earlier wrong rule, 13 had one wrong rule first, 9 had two or more wrong rules, 1 never announced a rule.
quote: no confirming instance of a law is a verifying instance, but that any disconfirming instance is a falsifying instance
limits: Small N, one rule, one culture and era. Wason called the behaviour enumerative induction. Later work (Wetherick 1962, Klayman and Ha 1987) says it is better read as positive testing than as a wish to confirm.
agent_relevance: A model that proposes a rule and then tests only inputs that fit it will stay stuck on a too-narrow rule. The scaffold must force at least one test from outside the current hypothesis.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task
finding: Design point: the universe of triples is infinite and the true rule is entailed by many obvious narrower rules. So confirming-only testing almost surely gives wrong conclusions. Earlier concept tasks (Bruner et al.) used finite stimulus sets, which hid the problem.
numbers: Wrong rules announced most often: increasing by 2, multiples of the first number, consecutive evens, arithmetic progression. Told their rule was wrong, subjects kept the same rule in more than half of cases and only changed the wording.
limits: Descriptive record. The wording-change finding comes from a few protocols, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Models also re-word a failed hypothesis instead of changing it. Code should compare the new hypothesis to the old one by what it predicts on test inputs, not by its text.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task
finding: Qualitative finding: some subjects restated the same rule in new words after being told it was wrong. Wason links this to the old result that a concept can be used before it can be put into words, and says insight into one's own thinking is often poor.
numbers: Three subjects repeated a single rule in different words across announcements; three reworded the rule right after being told it was wrong.
limits: Case protocols only, no counts beyond the three and three.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrail G10: stated reasoning is a weak record of what the thinker is doing. Judge by the tests it picks.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Core theory. Much of what is called confirmation bias is a positive test strategy (PTS): test cases you expect to have the target property. PTS is not the same as seeking to verify. Klayman and Ha separate a positive hypothesis test (+Htest, an instance the hypothesis says is a target) from a positive target test (+Ttest, an instance known to be a target).
numbers: Theory paper, no new sample. Example: in the 2-4-6 task the true rule (any increasing) has only about 1/6 of triples, assuming a large range of numbers.
quote: many phenomena labeled confirmation bias are better understood in terms of a general positive test strategy
limits: Analysis assumes a perfect target rule or known error rates. Their authors say PTS can still cause systematic errors.
agent_relevance: Name the test type in code: is this input predicted positive or negative by the current hypothesis? Then pick on purpose.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: The key formal result. When the hypothesis set H lies inside the true target set T (the 2-4-6 case), a +Htest can never falsify, because every such instance is in T. Only a negative test (an instance outside H) can show the rule is too narrow. In the reverse case (H bigger than T) the roles flip.
numbers: Table of outcomes: +Htest gives yes = ambiguous verification, no = impossible when H is inside T. -Htest gives yes = conclusive falsification, no = ambiguous verification.
limits: Applies to rule-discovery with one sided errors. The relation of H and T is usually unknown to the tester.
agent_relevance: This is the exact case for S7 select: a hypothesis that is a subset of the true rule can only be exposed by a test outside it. Code can build such an input, e.g. by perturbing the hypothesis.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: PTS is often the better choice for finding a falsification. The chance of a falsifying result from a +Htest versus a -Htest depends on the base rate p(t) of the target and the size of the hypothesis p(h). When p(h) is about p(t) and the target is a minority (p(t) below .5), positive tests are more likely to falsify than negative ones.
numbers: Equation 1: false-positive rate z+ = 1 - p(t)/p(h) (approximately); with p(h) about p(t) and p(t) < .5, z+ > z-. Cited base rates: schizophrenia under 1%, stars with planets about 1/10 to 1/6 in their sources, AIDS 10^-4 to 10^-5.
limits: Needs the tester to hold a decent estimate of p(t) and p(h) and a hypothesis of about the right size. Rule can reverse for majority phenomena.
agent_relevance: Test choice should depend on how rare the target is and how large the hypothesis is, not on a blanket call to falsify. A code-side estimate of those two sizes on sampled inputs can set test type.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Reviews what lifts 2-4-6 success. With more test chances and less time pressure people test more widely. Tweney et al. (1980) gave feedback as DAX (true rule) versus MED (everything else). People treated DAX and MED as two hypotheses and tested each positively, which fixed the problem.
numbers: No pooled figure given in the review; DAX/MED subjects used even fewer negative hypothesis tests than usual but still solved it more often (Tweney et al. 1980, as reported).
limits: Second-hand report of Tweney 1980; exact success counts were not opened.
agent_relevance: Reframing so that the feedback itself defines two competing hypotheses makes positive testing do falsification work. Ask for two complementary rules, not one.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Reads the four-card task through PTS. P and Q (or P alone) are the common answers because people use positive tests. But the rule if P then Q has only one way to be falsified (P and not-Q), so PTS is the wrong strategy there; only P and not-Q can reveal it. Concrete contexts like the beer and age 19 rule point people to the right cards.
numbers: Cites the beer-drinking problem (Griggs and Cox 1982) and pattern frequencies from Wason 1966, 1968; Evans and Lynch 1973 as most common P and Q, or P only.
limits: A one-sided conditional versus a two-sided rule is the key difference; PTS fits one and not the other.
agent_relevance: Before choosing a test, code should classify the rule type: one-way conditional (look for the counterexample P and not-Q) or two-way (positive tests may suffice).

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: Concept identification with a small finite hypothesis set allows the focusing strategy (Bruner et al.), which is optimal, but costs effort and memory. People instead use win-stay, lose-shift with positive tests. Their thesis: when task detail is missing or load is high, people default to PTS.
numbers: Example set: 4 binary cues give 8 one-feature hypotheses; one trial can drop 4 rules at once.
limits: Argument, not a measured effect size.
agent_relevance: Where the hypothesis set is small and listable, code can do elimination bookkeeping that people cannot, and pick the input that splits the set.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: Reframes the selection task as choosing data to tell two hypotheses apart: a dependence model (if p then q) and an independence model. Each card is scored by expected reduction in Shannon uncertainty (expected information gain, EIG). With the rarity assumption (p and q are rare in the world), EIG orders cards p > q > not-q > not-p, which matches the common choices.
numbers: Card EIG: p informative when P(q) is low; q when P(p) and P(q) are both small; not-q to the extent P(p) is large; not-p is zero. Prior P(MD)=.5. Meta-analysis: 13 studies, 34 abstract tasks, 845 subjects.
limits: EIG with rarity is a computational-level claim. It was challenged on psychological plausibility, probabilities assumed, and fit (see a13 to a15).
agent_relevance: An EIG calculation is something code can run for any pair of surviving hypotheses. It gives a principled ordering of candidate tests, instead of a vote.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: Baseline facts on the abstract task. Few give the logical answer. Pooled card choice rates across 34 tasks: p 89%, q 62%, not-q 25%, not-p 16%.
numbers: Pattern rates quoted from Johnson-Laird and Wason (1970a): p and q 46%, p only 33%, p, q and not-q 7%, p and not-q (logical) 4%. Pooled counts of 845 subjects: p 754, q 522, not-q 215, not-p 137.
quote: only 4% of subjects make this response
limits: The 4% is one early study; other sources give 5 to 10%. Pooled rates are from affirmative abstract rules only.
agent_relevance: The reference rate for the naive answer is very low. A plain model will likely show a similar bias if the prompt gives a conditional with no content cue; test this.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: The model explains other variants. The reduced array task (RAST, where people choose q or not-q items and see data) makes the rule's domain explicit so P(q) is about .5. That breaks rarity and the model then predicts more not-q picks, which is seen. The negations paradigm is explained by raising the subjective probabilities of negated categories.
numbers: Original model: with P(p)=.1 to rare values, EIG(q) > EIG(not-q) only in the region where both are small.
limits: Needs parameters such as rarity values to be set after the fact for some data.
agent_relevance: Which test is best depends on how the sampled input space is divided. Code can tell the model the true sizes of the sets.

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Revised the model: both hypotheses now share the same marginals, and an exceptions parameter allows an imperfect dependency. Compared against mental logic (PSYCOP), mental models and others on 34 studies. The revised information gain model was not rejected overall, and fit as well as or better than its rivals.
numbers: Across 34 studies the model could not be rejected, G2(68)=88.37. Best-fit mean P(p)=.22 (SE .019) and mean P(q)=.27. Individual-rule fits: not-p then q, G2(12)=16.07; not-p then not-q, G2(12)=13.68.
quote: some version of the optimal data selection model still provides the best account of the selection task
limits: Authors of the model are the ones who wrote the comparison. Parameters P(p), P(q) free per study. Others contest the fits.
agent_relevance: Even when a rival fits, the point stands that tests can be ranked by information; the exact descriptive fit matters less for the scaffold.

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Direct tests of the model's novel predictions. Changing P(q) changes card choice: as P(q) rises, not-q picks rise and q picks fall. Equal-size stacks were used to rule out a small-stack bias. In the standard four-card task, manipulating antecedent and consequent probabilities gave results in line with the model.
numbers: Oaksford, Chater, Grainger and Larkin (1997) Exp. 1 and Exp. 3 (equal stacks) agreed. Oaksford, Chater and Grainger (1999): four experiments, 28 conditions, mean G2(2)=3.15, none rejected; but not-q picks never passed q picks in Exp. 1 with real-world content.
limits: The authors concede probability manipulations with real-world content were only partly successful, as prior beliefs interfere.
agent_relevance: Test choice shifts with the stated frequencies of the categories. Tell the agent the frequencies explicitly (from code) rather than let it guess.

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Records the critics and the failed or mixed tests. Laming (1996), Evans and Over (1996), Oberauer et al. (1999), Gebauer and Laming (1997), Green (2000) and Hardman (1998) argued against it. Oberauer et al. failed to find probability effects in their experiments; the authors answer that those used small samples and other differences.
numbers: Authors cite Stanovich and West (1998): at most 10% of university students can engage System 2 processes on this task. Green and Over (1997): about 70% wanted to see some of all four classes of patients, more of p and q than not-p and not-q.
quote: at most, 10% of university students are capable of engaging System 2 processes
limits: The rebuttal is by the model's authors; independent replication of probability effects was mixed.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one account is settled. The safe design is: let code compute information value, and do not trust the model's own claim of what is informative.

source: Cosmides (1989) The logic of social exchange: Has natural selection shaped how humans reason?
finding: Social contract theory. If a rule has a cost-benefit structure (take a benefit only if you pay the cost), people check for cheaters (benefit taken, cost not paid), even on unfamiliar rules. That gives the logical answer on a content where the logic of if-then alone does not.
numbers: Unfamiliar social contracts vs matched descriptive rules, correct P and not-Q: Exp. 1 75% vs 21%, F(1,23)=27.18; Exp. 2 71% vs 25%. Descriptive with abstract control: 75% vs 25% (Exp. 1) and 71% vs 29% (Exp. 2). Familiar rule baseline (drinking age): 78%. Abstract tasks usually 10% or less.
limits: Sample about 24 to 40 per experiment, Stanford students. Later critics argue the effect can come from deontic or relevance cues, not a special module.
agent_relevance: The same logical rule is solved or missed depending on how the case is framed. A frame that names a violation (benefit taken, cost not paid) makes the counterexample case obvious.

source: Cosmides (1989) The logic of social exchange: Has natural selection shaped how humans reason?
finding: Switched social contract test. Swapping the order of the clauses should flip the right answer to not-P and Q (the cheater cards), as in social contract theory, but not as in a permission-schema account that tracks the form of the rule. People gave the cheater-detection answer even when it was logically wrong for the form.
numbers: Switched social contracts vs non-social-contract permission rules, not-P and Q: Exp. 8 65% vs 0%, Z=4.39; Exp. 9 80% vs 10%, Z=4.45. Context-only (social purpose) vs no-context rules: 85 to 90% vs 55 to 60% (earlier study noted in paper).
limits: Original work from one lab; Cheng and Holyoak (1989) answered that the data fit permission or obligation schemas too.
agent_relevance: Models trained on human text may have a similar cheater-style frame as a shortcut. The scaffold should not assume the pattern holds for all conditionals.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Tests permission and obligation framings in abstract form against adaptive (precaution, social contract) framings and matched controls. Abstract deontic framings helped little. Adaptive framings helped more.
numbers: Three groups of 20 naive subjects. Correct: precaution 50%, social contract 45%, obligation 30%, permission 20%, situation control 15%, action control 10%. Adaptive 48% vs deontic 25% overall; deontic not significantly above matched controls.
limits: N=20 per group; Fiddick works inside the evolutionary camp. Cheng and Holyoak's original abstract permission problem: 61% vs 19% correct (reported in this paper).
agent_relevance: The facilitation effect depends on the content frame, not on the label deontic. For a model, an explicit violation frame (who is cheating, what is the danger) is likely worth more than the word rule.

source: Cheng and Holyoak (1985) Pragmatic reasoning schemas
finding: Proposed pragmatic reasoning schemas, such as permission (if action, then precondition). Evoking the permission schema improved the selection task for subjects with no experience of the specific content. Abstract permission wording beat concrete wording in Exp. 2.
numbers: As reported in Fiddick (2003): 61% correct on the abstract permission problem vs 19% on the non-deontic control (Exp. 2). Not read in the original.
limits: Not opened this session (PDF did not download). Figures are second-hand. Jackson and Griggs (1990) found the effect fragile to wording; Noveck and O'Brien (1996) found instruction effects.
agent_relevance: Rule type matters: permission and obligation rules cue the violation case. A classifier in code can detect these and switch the test prompt.

source: Sperber, Cara and Girotto (1995) Relevance theory explains the selection task
finding: Relevance account. People infer consequences of the rule in order of accessibility and stop when the result meets their expectation of relevance. So they pick whatever cards the interpretation makes relevant. Correct answers can be elicited in any content domain by raising expectations of relevance, even for abstract material.
numbers: Exp. 1 (virgin mothers, n=27 per condition): P and not-Q in 21 of 27 (78%) relevance condition vs 7 of 27 (26%) irrelevance. Exp. 3 (unemployment): 70% vs 25%. Exp. 4 (abstract machine problem): 57% correct in the effect-plus, effort-minus condition; 38% in two partial conditions.
limits: Student samples around 27 per cell. Oaksford and Chater (1995) replied that relevance and information gain are compatible, not rival.
agent_relevance: What the model reads as the point of the rule drives which case it checks. State the goal as finding a violation and lower the reading effort of the not-Q case.

source: Sperber, Cara and Girotto (1995) Relevance theory explains the selection task
finding: Review of the historical record. About 90% of subjects fail the standard task. Two variants succeed: a negated consequent (if P then not Q, about 60% correct per Evans 1972) and thematic rules such as the drinking-age rule. They also cite Legrenzi (1970), where almost 80% solved a thematic version.
numbers: Standard task: about 10% correct. Negated consequent: about 60% correct (Evans 1972, as cited). More than 90% of selections in standard versions include the P card.
limits: Second-hand citations; each original not opened. Negated-consequent success is generally attributed to matching bias, not insight.
agent_relevance: A correct answer can come from matching the words in the rule, not from understanding. Check candidate answers on a changed-wording version of the same problem.

source: Stahl, Klauer and Erdfelder (2008) Matching bias in the selection task is not eliminated by explicit negations
finding: Large online replication in the negations paradigm. Matching bias (picking the cards named in the rule, regardless of negation) was strong with implicit negations. With explicit negations it was reduced but not eliminated, against earlier claims. Model analysis says negations push people toward a negative test strategy.
numbers: Two web experiments; Exp. 1 groups of about 300 to 350 each (336, 300, 341, 349), Exp. 2 groups of 200 to 360 each. About 75% of data fit the inference submodel and about 25% the guessing submodel in a related model fit.
quote: matching bias was reduced but not eliminated in conditions using explicit negations
limits: Online, self-selected sample. Estimate of 75/25 came from the model, not directly from observation.
agent_relevance: The surface form of a rule (negations) changes which cards are chosen. Test the agent on negated rewordings to catch matching rather than reasoning.

source: Nickerson (1998) Confirmation bias: A ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises
finding: Reviews confirmation bias and separates logical from psychological confirmation. A yes to a triple chosen to fit your guess feels like strong confirmation but is often not logically strong. Wetherick (1962) argued that we cannot tell whether a person aims to eliminate a hypothesis unless we know what they intended with each test. Wason (1962, 1968) replied that even intelligent people hold to their hypotheses with remarkable tenacity.
numbers: Review, no new data.
quote: even intelligent individuals adhere to their own hypotheses with remarkable tenacity
limits: Narrative review; some of the evidence is of mixed quality.
agent_relevance: Log the intent of each test with the test (what hypothesis it is meant to separate) so code can check if a test could have failed.

source: Nickerson (1998) Confirmation bias: A ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises
finding: Argues that choosing A and 4 in the four-card task is not avoiding falsification: A can falsify the rule. The only way to avoid falsification is to choose B or 4. The task has two readings: which of these four cards to turn (answer P and not-Q) versus which types of evidence best test the rule in general, where P may be the only informative choice and not-Q may be nearly pointless when it is rare.
numbers: No new figures.
limits: Nickerson's own interpretation, supported by Kirby 1994 and Oaksford and Chater 1994.
agent_relevance: State in the prompt which question the agent must answer: check these given items, or design the best test from a class. The best test differs.

source: Nickerson (1998) Confirmation bias: A ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises
finding: Summary of content effects. Performance is better with familiar situational content and with deontic rules (permission, obligation, promise) than with indicative rules. People find modus tollens less natural than modus ponens, which fits the weak not-Q choice.
numbers: Cites many sources (Johnson-Laird, Legrenzi and Legrenzi 1972; Wason and Shapiro 1971; Cheng and Holyoak 1985; Cosmides 1989; Griggs and Cox; Manktelow and Over 1990, 1991); no pooled effect size is given.
limits: Citations summarised, originals not opened. Einhorn and Hogarth (1978) found thematic content is not always perfect.
agent_relevance: Add a modus tollens style check as an explicit operator: for a conditional claim, derive and test the contrapositive case.

source: Gale and Ball (2006) Dual-goal facilitation in Wason's 2-4-6 task: What mediates successful rule discovery?
finding: Asking people to find two rules, DAX and MED, in the 2-4-6 task raises success. The effect appears whatever the rule labels are.
numbers: As reported in a search summary, not read: about 20% success in the standard task; above 60% in the dual-goal version.
limits: Abstract and summary only. Full text not opened. Later paper (2009) says perfect rule complementarity is not needed.
agent_relevance: A two-hypothesis framing is a cheap prompt-side lever. Test it against a plain single-rule prompt at equal tokens.

source: Ragni, Kola and Johnson-Laird (2018) On selecting evidence to test hypotheses: A theory of selection tasks
finding: Meta-analysis of 228 selection task experiments compared 16 theories. Selections within an experiment depend on one another more than chance. Salient counterexamples raise their selection. The mental model theory fit best; Kellen and Klauer (2020) argued the model comparison is non-identifiable.
numbers: As reported in a search summary, not read: 228 experiments; in 99 of them selections were more redundant than 10,000 simulated independent runs.
limits: Not opened; the authors favour their own theory; the critique was published in Computational Brain and Behavior (2020).
agent_relevance: Salience of the counterexample matters. The scaffold should state the counterexample case outright instead of hoping the model finds it.

source: Evans and Lynch (1973) Matching bias in the selection task
finding: Negations paradigm. People tend to pick the cards named in the rule regardless of whether the logic needs them, so negated rules (if P then not Q) look easier. Taken as evidence for a non-logical heuristic.
numbers: Search summary, not read: 61% gave the correct answer in one negated version.
limits: Search snippet only. Stahl et al. (2008, a22) show the effect persists but shrinks with explicit negations.
agent_relevance: Cheap diagnostic for matching: reword the same logic with negations and see if the agent flips its answer.

source: Evans and Over (1996) Rationality in the selection task: Epistemic utility versus uncertainty reduction
finding: Critique of the information gain model. Argues expected information gain is both psychologically implausible and not a good measure of epistemic utility for the task.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Only the abstract-level description from a search was seen; Oaksford and Chater (2003) summarise the reply.
agent_relevance: Information gain is only one candidate for ranking tests; utility of a test (what we do with the answer) also counts.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987), Nickerson (1998) and Oaksford and Chater (1994) combined reading
finding: Three accounts of the same behaviour agree on the practical rule even though they disagree on psychology. Falsification is not always the best test. The best test is the one most likely to split the live hypotheses, given how big each is and how rare the target is. Where one hypothesis sits inside another, only a test outside the smaller one can tell them apart.
numbers: No single figure; see a05, a06, a10.
limits: This is our synthesis across three opened sources, not a claim any author makes in these words.
agent_relevance: Operator for S7: code lists live hypotheses, builds the input where they disagree (a counterexample search), runs it, and drops the losers. Compare against a vote at equal tokens (guardrail G7).
